prompts:
This is an instructional notebook. It is the appendix notebook on the dataset used in part 1 of the course "Tabular Foundation Models with TabICL".

Content: loads the Capital Bikeshare data (Washington D.C., hourly, 2011 and 2012) from OpenML, explores it and saves the CSV that the part 1 notebooks load. Columns: `season`, `year` (0 for 2011, 1 for 2012), `month`, `hour`, `weekday`, `holiday`, `workingday`, `weather`, `temp`, `feel_temp`, `humidity`, `windspeed`, and the target `count`, the number of bikes rented that hour; `season`, `holiday`, `workingday` and `weather` are categorical. Findings: on working days, demand peaks around 8 a.m. and 5 to 6 p.m., while on weekends it rises through the morning and stays high all afternoon, an interaction between `hour` and `workingday`. Demand grows over the two years (about 235 rentals per hour in 2012 against 144 in 2011), which is one reason why the course always tests on hours after the training hours, and it is lower in winter. Rain roughly halves demand; `heavy_rain` occurs in only 3 hours. The target is skewed, most hours below 300 and a maximum of 977. A few hours are missing; using the `hour` column, the data splits into 76 stretches of consecutive hours, the longest from April to October 2012. The saved data keeps every hour up to the end of that stretch, dropping the last 1,495 hours, so that every test window of the course spans consecutive hours and the 48-hour gap really is 48 hours. A CSV does not keep pandas dtypes, so the other notebooks convert the categorical columns back after loading. In the browser, `fetch_openml` may need `pyodide_http.patch_urllib()` to download the data.
